slide_drafts.speaker_notes: Now let me address the strategic imperative. Japan's research funding crisis is not speculation—it is arithmetic. The KAKENHI budget has remained around 240 billion yen annually, but the number of applications has grown substantially. Adjusted for inflation and the weakening yen, the average funding per project has effectively halved since 2013. Publication fees, conference travel, and equipment costs have all risen. National university operating grants have been cut by approximately 140 billion yen cumulatively since the 2004 corporatization, with a 1% annual efficiency coefficient that systematically erodes budgets. This is the environment we operate in. The question is not whether to seek alternative funding—it is where.

slide_drafts.speaker_notes: The severity of this crisis is recognized at the highest levels. In July 2024, 167 academic associations representing 2.08 million researchers petitioned the government to double KAKENHI funding to more than 480 billion yen. The Nature Index 2024 shows Japan's adjusted share declining 9% year-over-year. Both the University of Tokyo and Kyoto University recorded their lowest rankings to date—with Kyoto falling outside the top 50 for the first time since the index began. Yet as RIKEN President Gonokami acknowledged, doubling the budget is unlikely under the current system. The institutional response will be slow. Individual researchers cannot wait. Diversification is not abandonment of domestic funding—it is prudent risk management.
